policydecision_details:
Under the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since the 2003 reform, the EU provides direct support to its farmers in the form of payments granted directly to them under certain support schemes. These include: the single payment scheme (SPS), the single area payment scheme (SAPS), and support schemes for farmers producing rice, starch potatoes, protein crops, nuts, seeds, cotton, sugar, fruit and vegetables, sheepmeat and goatmeal and veal and beef. Direct support of the EU is currently based on Council Regulation (EC) No 73/2009. The objective of the EU direct support is to provide a safety net for farmers in the form of a basic income as well as contribute to providing basic public goods delivered through sustainable farming. The budgetary ceilings for these direct support measures change every year. The yearly budget allocated by the EU is of around €40 billion.

The SPS entered into force in 2005 and is implemented by 17 countries of the EU, with the other 10 implementing the SAPS. 
The SAPS was offered as an option for countries joining the EU in 2004 and 2007 and will remain in force until 2013. It is a transition measure towards implementing the SPS. For the SAPS, the level of payment is calculated by dividing the country’s annual financial envelope by its respective utilized agricultural area. Under the SPS, support is granted in the form of a single annual payment dependent on the entitlement of the farmers. The three main options for calculating the value of payment entitlements include a historical, regional, and hybrid model. The historical model is based on the payments received by a farmer during a reference period, resulting in different aid levels per hectare. The regional model takes all payments received in a region and divides them by the number of eligible hectares, resulting in a flat rate. The hybrid model is made up of a mixture of the 2 other models. 
Cross-compliance ties the direct support for farmers with standards of environmental care, public/animal/plant health and animal welfare, penalising farmers who infringe EU law by reducing the support they receive. Cross-compliance covers directives and regulations which formulate “statutory management requirements”, which apply to all farmers, even if they are not receiving direct support from the EU. In order to help farmers better understand and meet the EU rules set up by cross compliance, every member state has established a Farm Advisory System. 

In addition to this, the EU established a set of rules on good agricultural and environmental conditions which farmers must comply with in order to receive payments under the CAP. 

The CAP reform in 2003 decoupled direct support to farmers, so that payments were no longer linked to production of a specific product. Up to 10% of the budget allocated for each Member states, is made available to support specific sectors for the purposes of: 
1) Protecting or enhancing the environment
2) Improving the quality of agricultural products,
3) Improving the marketing of agricultural products,
4) Practicing enhanced animal welfare standards,
5) Specific agricultural activities entailing additional agro-environment benefits
6) Payments for disadvantages affecting farmers in specific sectors (dairy, beef, veal, sheep and goat and rice) in economically or environmentally sensitive areas as well as for economically vulnerable types of farming,
7) Top-ups to existing Single Payment Scheme payment entitlements in areas where land abandonment is a threat
8) Support for risk assurance in the form of contributions to crop, animal and plant insurance premia
9) Support by way of mutual funds for animal and plant diseases and environmental incidents.

From 2012 at the latest, all of these coupled payments will be decoupled and integrated into the SPS, except for the suckler cows, sheep and goat and cotton schemes which may remain linked to the production of those products.

policydecision_details:
Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) regulates animal health and welfare. This is based upon Article 13 of the Treaty of the Functioning of the European Union which recognises animals as sentient beings and requires full regard to be given to the welfare requirements of animals. Council Directive 2002/99/EC is the main legislation with regards to animal health and welfare. Countries within the EU may choose to implement stricter regulations, providing that they are compatible with those set out in the Treaty. The regulations cover the protection of animals during transport, at the time of slaughter and killing, protection of animals for scientific and experimental purposes, and the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. The principle which EU law with regards to animal welfare is based upon include freedom from discomfort, hunger, thirst, fear, distress, pain, injury, disease, and the freedom to express natural behaviour. 
This Animal Health Strategy has 4 main objectives of ensuring a high level of public health and food safety, supporting farming and the rural economy, improving economic growth/cohesion/competitiveness, and to promote farming practices and animal welfare which prevent animal health related threats and minimise environmental impacts.

policydecision_details:
Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has been regulating plant health and variety. The main legislation with regards to plant health and variety is Council Directive 2000/29/EC (amending Council Directive 77/93/EEC).
The main objective of EU plant health legislation is to protect the safety of food derived from plants and to secure the health and quality status of crops in the EU. The legislation regulates the trade of plants and plant products within the EU as well as imports from the rest of the world in accordance with international plant health standards and obligations. This is partially done through providing protective measures against the spread of harmful organisms. The legislation contains a list of harmful organisms that threaten plant health in the EU. This includes the establishment of the European Union Notification System for Plant Health Interceptions (EUROPHYT), which is a rapid alert system dealing with interceptions for plant health reasons of plants and plant products imported into the EU or being traded within the EU itself. EUROPHYT also contributes to the implementation of preventative measures by ensuring that the data on risks to plant and plant products is up-to-date and accurate. 
The legislation with regards to plant health is known as the Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR). The Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR) looks towards contributing to sustainable production through plant health protection; ensuring competitiveness of the agriculture complex; contribute to the protection of public and private green, forests, and the landscape, and to ensure food security. 
The selling and use of plant protection products and their residue in food is also regulated.  Council Directive 91/414/EEC is concerned with the placing of plant protection products on the market. No plant protection product may be used within the EU unless it has been scientifically established that the products have no harmful effects on consumers, farmers, and local residents and passers-by; they do not cause unacceptable effects on the environment; and that they are sufficiently effective against pests. 
Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 currently governs the maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides in food and feed in order to protect the health of consumers. These are controlled by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). If any infringements of the Regulation are found, these shall be countered by sanctions of the product.

The main legislation which sets out the rules with regards to the POSEI programmes is Council Regulation (EC) No 247/2006. These programmes are designed to take account of their geographical and economic handicaps, such as remoteness, insularity, small size, difficult topography and climate, and economic dependence on a few products. The programme functions by specific supply arrangements, aimed at mitigating the additional costs for the supply of essential products for human consumption, for processing and as agricultural inputs, and measures to support the local agricultural production.

This is due to the high input of raw material prices in the EU, which may cause the prices for certain farm products in the EU to be higher than the world price level for the same product. Export refunds are provided to exporters who must export their farmed goods to third countries, to bridge the gap between the EU price level and the world price level, to help them to better compete on world markets. The values for the refunds must be fixed at least once every three months; however these can stay the same for longer than three months. policydecision_details:
Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has established laws and regulations to govern the use and development of bio-technology. A major concern for the EU with regards to bio-technology is genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which is mainly regulated by Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. The main objectives for these regulations are to protect human and animal health by introducing a safety assessment of the highest possible standards at EU level before any genetically modified (GM) food and feed is placed on the market; to have in place harmonised procedures for risk assessment and authorisation of GM food and feed that are efficient, time-limited and transparent; to ensure clear labelling of GM food and feed in order to respond to consumers’ concern and enable them to make an informed choice and to avoid misleading consumers; to set labelling requirements for GM feed which provide farmers with accurate information on the composition and properties of feed, thereby enabling them to make an informed choice. In order for GM food or feed to be allowed onto the European Market, it must go through an authorisation procedure. The first step in the procedure is the submission of an application for an authorisation for the placing on the market, which is followed by the preparation and the delivery of an opinion by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The public is then allowed to make comments on the opinion, after which the European Commission prepares and adopts a decision.
EU legislation allows for countries within the EU to provisionally restrict or prohibit the use and/or sale of the GM product on its territory. Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Germany, and Luxembourg have applied this safeguard measure to certain GM products within their territory.

policydecision_details:
Under the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since the 2003 reform, the EU provides direct support to its farmers in the form of payments granted directly to them under certain support schemes. These include: the single payment scheme (SPS), the single area payment scheme (SAPS), and support schemes for farmers producing rice, starch potatoes, protein crops, nuts, seeds, cotton, sugar, fruit and vegetables, sheepmeat and goatmeal and veal and beef. Direct support of the EU is currently based on Council Regulation (EC) No 73/2009. The objective of the EU direct support is to provide a safety net for farmers in the form of a basic income as well as contribute to providing basic public goods delivered through sustainable farming. The budgetary ceilings for these direct support measures change every year. The yearly budget allocated by the EU is of around €40 billion.

The SPS entered into force in 2005 and is implemented by 17 countries of the EU, with the other 10 implementing the SAPS. 
The SAPS was offered as an option for countries joining the EU in 2004 and 2007 and will remain in force until 2013. It is a transition measure towards implementing the SPS. For the SAPS, the level of payment is calculated by dividing the country’s annual financial envelope by its respective utilized agricultural area. Under the SPS, support is granted in the form of a single annual payment dependent on the entitlement of the farmers. The three main options for calculating the value of payment entitlements include a historical, regional, and hybrid model. The historical model is based on the payments received by a farmer during a reference period, resulting in different aid levels per hectare. The regional model takes all payments received in a region and divides them by the number of eligible hectares, resulting in a flat rate. The hybrid model is made up of a mixture of the 2 other models. 
Cross-compliance ties the direct support for farmers with standards of environmental care, public/animal/plant health and animal welfare, penalising farmers who infringe EU law by reducing the support they receive. Cross-compliance covers directives and regulations which formulate “statutory management requirements”, which apply to all farmers, even if they are not receiving direct support from the EU. In order to help farmers better understand and meet the EU rules set up by cross compliance, every member state has established a Farm Advisory System. 

In addition to this, the EU established a set of rules on good agricultural and environmental conditions which farmers must comply with in order to receive payments under the CAP. 

The CAP reform in 2003 decoupled direct support to farmers, so that payments were no longer linked to production of a specific product. Up to 10% of the budget allocated for each Member states, is made available to support specific sectors for the purposes of: 
1) Protecting or enhancing the environment
2) Improving the quality of agricultural products,
3) Improving the marketing of agricultural products,
4) Practicing enhanced animal welfare standards,
5) Specific agricultural activities entailing additional agro-environment benefits
6) Payments for disadvantages affecting farmers in specific sectors (dairy, beef, veal, sheep and goat and rice) in economically or environmentally sensitive areas as well as for economically vulnerable types of farming,
7) Top-ups to existing Single Payment Scheme payment entitlements in areas where land abandonment is a threat
8) Support for risk assurance in the form of contributions to crop, animal and plant insurance premia
9) Support by way of mutual funds for animal and plant diseases and environmental incidents.

From 2012 at the latest, all of these coupled payments will be decoupled and integrated into the SPS, except for the suckler cows, sheep and goat and cotton schemes which may remain linked to the production of those products.

policydecision_details:
Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has been regulating plant health and variety. The main legislation with regards to plant health and variety is Council Directive 2000/29/EC (amending Council Directive 77/93/EEC).
The main objective of EU plant health legislation is to protect the safety of food derived from plants and to secure the health and quality status of crops in the EU. The legislation regulates the trade of plants and plant products within the EU as well as imports from the rest of the world in accordance with international plant health standards and obligations. This is partially done through providing protective measures against the spread of harmful organisms. The legislation contains a list of harmful organisms that threaten plant health in the EU. This includes the establishment of the European Union Notification System for Plant Health Interceptions (EUROPHYT), which is a rapid alert system dealing with interceptions for plant health reasons of plants and plant products imported into the EU or being traded within the EU itself. EUROPHYT also contributes to the implementation of preventative measures by ensuring that the data on risks to plant and plant products is up-to-date and accurate. 
The legislation with regards to plant health is known as the Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR). The Common Plant Health Regime (CPHR) looks towards contributing to sustainable production through plant health protection; ensuring competitiveness of the agriculture complex; contribute to the protection of public and private green, forests, and the landscape, and to ensure food security. 
The selling and use of plant protection products and their residue in food is also regulated.  Council Directive 91/414/EEC is concerned with the placing of plant protection products on the market. No plant protection product may be used within the EU unless it has been scientifically established that the products have no harmful effects on consumers, farmers, and local residents and passers-by; they do not cause unacceptable effects on the environment; and that they are sufficiently effective against pests. 
Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 currently governs the maximum residue levels (MRLs) of pesticides in food and feed in order to protect the health of consumers. These are controlled by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). If any infringements of the Regulation are found, these shall be countered by sanctions of the product.

Council Regulation (EC) No 2100/94 covers the intellectual property rights, known as the Community Plant Variety Right (CPVR,) granted to plant varieties. The CPVR is granted to the person who bred, or discovered and developed a new plant variety or his successor. However these varieties must be distinct, uniform, stable, and new. Any production or reproduction, conditioning for the purpose of propagation, offering for sale, selling or marketing, exporting from the community, exporting from the Community, importing from the Community, or stocking for any of the previously mentioned purposes, will therefore require the authorization of the holder of the CPVR for that variety. policydecision_details:
EU fruit and vegetable scheme – Romania

The EU School Fruit Scheme, launched in the 2009-2010 school year, merged with the EU School Milk Scheme on 1 August 2017 into one legal framework based on the Regulation on the new School Fruit, Vegetables and Milk Scheme (Regulation EU No 2016/791). The scheme is funded through the EU’s common agricultural policy and supports the distribution of fruit, vegetables and milk and milk products to schools across the EU as part of a wider programme of education about European agriculture and the benefits of healthy eating. It provides financing to Member States based on the number of school children and level of development of the country. The implementation of the programmes is at the discretion of national or regional governments, but to receive funding, they must distribute fruit, vegetables and milk products in schools and implement educational measures, such as farm and market visits, educational material distributed to teachers and interactive games on education and nutrition, and regularly monitor and evaluate implementation. Foods containing added sugars, salt, fat, sweeteners or artificial flavor enhances are exempt from the scheme: as an exception, limited quantities of added sugar, salt and fat are allowed if they are approved by the Member States' health/nutrition authorities. The Member States determine the frequency and duration of the distribution of the food.

Regulation 1924/2006 establishes EU-wide rules on the use of specified nutrient content and comparative claims (ie levels of fat for a low-fat claim). As of January 2010, only nutrition claims as listed in the Regulation’s annex are permitted. In theory, these nutrition claims may only be used on food defined as "healthy" by a nutrient profile. Therefore, permitted nutrition claims can be used as long as the conditions for use of the claim as set out in the annex are met. policydecision_details:
Within the framework of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the European Union (EU) has established laws and regulations to govern the use and development of bio-technology. A major concern for the EU with regards to bio-technology is genetically modified organisms (GMOs), which is mainly regulated by Regulation (EC) No 1829/2003. The main objectives for these regulations are to protect human and animal health by introducing a safety assessment of the highest possible standards at EU level before any genetically modified (GM) food and feed is placed on the market; to have in place harmonised procedures for risk assessment and authorisation of GM food and feed that are efficient, time-limited and transparent; to ensure clear labelling of GM food and feed in order to respond to consumers’ concern and enable them to make an informed choice and to avoid misleading consumers; to set labelling requirements for GM feed which provide farmers with accurate information on the composition and properties of feed, thereby enabling them to make an informed choice. In order for GM food or feed to be allowed onto the European Market, it must go through an authorisation procedure. The first step in the procedure is the submission of an application for an authorisation for the placing on the market, which is followed by the preparation and the delivery of an opinion by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The public is then allowed to make comments on the opinion, after which the European Commission prepares and adopts a decision.
EU legislation allows for countries within the EU to provisionally restrict or prohibit the use and/or sale of the GM product on its territory. Austria, France, Greece, Hungary, Germany, and Luxembourg have applied this safeguard measure to certain GM products within their territory.

The government approved the Concept of the demographic policy of the Far East for the period until 2025 (hereinafter - the Concept).

The concept defines the goals, objectives, mechanisms and main directions of state policy in the field of demographic development of the constituent entities of the Federation included in the Far Eastern Federal District, and is aimed at stabilizing the population of the Far East by 2020 and creating conditions for its natural and migratory growth by 2025.

The concept provides:

- population growth up to 6.5 million people due to natural and migration growth, attracting to the regions of the Far East for permanent residence of residents of other regions, compatriots living abroad, qualified foreign specialists and young people;

- increase the value of the total birth rate to 2.05; reduction of mortality from all causes to the level of 11.5 cases per 1 thousand people;

- increase in life expectancy up to 74.2 years;

- creating conditions for a further increase in the population of the Far East to 7 million people.

The concept contains the values ​​of the main demographic indicators for 2017–2025 in the context of the constituent entities of the Federation included in the Far Eastern Federal District, which are determined on the basis of proposals from the executive authorities of these regions.

The concept is planned to be implemented in two stages.

At the first stage (2017–2020), a set of measures is envisaged aimed at improving the demographic situation and stabilizing the population of the Far East.

At the second stage (2021–2025), actions are planned to ensure a natural and migratory increase in the population of the Far East.
policy_description: Concept of demographic policy of the Far East

Strategic Goals:

11.1. Strategic Goal A: Address the underlying causes of biodiversity loss by mainstreaming biodiversity across government and society
11.1.1 Global target 1 – By 2020, at the latest, people are aware of the values of biodiversity and the steps they can take to conserve and use it sustainably
11.1.2 Global target 2 – By 2020, at the latest, biodiversity values have been integrated into national and local development and poverty reduction strategies and planning processes and are being incorporated into national accounting, as appropriate, and reporting systems
11.1.3 Global target 3 – By 2020, at the latest, incentives, including subsidies, harmful to biodiversity are eliminated, phased out or reformed in order to minimize or avoid negative impacts, and positive incentives for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity are developed and applied, consistent and in harmony with the Convention and other relevant international obligations, taking into account national socio-economic conditions
11.1.4 Global target 4 – By 2020, at the latest, Governments, business and stakeholders at all levels have taken steps to achieve or have implemented plans for sustainable production and consumption and have kept the impacts of use of natural resources well within safe ecological limits
11.2. Strategic Goal B: Reduce the direct pressures on biodiversity and promote sustainable use
11.2.1 Global target 5 – By 2020, the rate of loss of all natural habitats, including forests, is at least halved and where feasible brought close to zero, and degradation and fragmentation is significantly reduced
11.2.2 Global Target 6 – By 2020 all fish and invertebrate stocks and aquatic plants are managed and harvested sustainably, legally and applying ecosystem based approaches, so that overfishing is avoided, recovery plans and measures are in place for all depleted species, fisheries have no significant adverse impacts on threatened species and vulnerable ecosystems and the impacts of fisheries on stocks, species and ecosystems are within safe ecological limits 
11.2.3 Global target 7 – By 2020 areas under agriculture, aquaculture and forestry are managed sustainably, ensuring conservation of biodiversity 
11.2.4 Global target 8 – By 2020, pollution, including from excess nutrients, has been brought to levels that are not detrimental to ecosystem function and biodiversity 
11.2.5 Global target 9 – By 2020, invasive alien species and pathways are identified and prioritized, priority species are controlled or eradicated, and measures are in place to manage pathways to prevent their introduction and establishment 
11.2.6 Global target 10 – By 2015, the multiple anthropogenic pressures on coral reefs, and other vulnerable ecosystems impacted by climate change or ocean acidification are minimized, so as to maintain their integrity and functioning 
11.3. Strategic Goal C: Improve the status of biodiversity by safeguarding ecosystems, species and genetic diversity 
11.3.1 Global target 11 – By 2020, at least 17 per cent of terrestrial and inland water, and 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas, especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem services, are conserved through effectively and equitably managed, ecologically representative and well connected systems of protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures, and integrated into the wider landscape and seascapes 
11.3.2 Global target 12 – By 2020, the genetic diversity of cultivated plants and farmed and domesticated animals and of wild relatives, including other socio-economically as well as culturally valuable species, is maintained, and strategies have been developed and implemented for minimizing genetic erosion and safeguarding their genetic diversity
11.2.2 11.3.2 Global target 13: By 2020, the genetic diversity of cultivated plants and farmed and domesticated animals and of wild relatives, including other socio-economically as well as culturally valuable species, is maintained, and strategies have been developed and implemented for minimizing genetic erosion and safeguarding their genetic diversity
11.4. Strategic Goal D: Enhance the benefits to all from biodiversity and ecosystem services
11.4.1 Global target 14 – By 2020, ecosystems that provide essential services, including services related to water, and contribute to health, livelihoods and wellbeing, are restored and safeguarded, taking into account the needs of women, indigenous and local communities, and the poor and vulnerable
11.4.2. Global target 15 – By 2020, ecosystem resilience and the contribution of biodiversity to carbon stocks has been enhanced, through conservation and restoration, including restoration of at least 15 per cent of degraded ecosystems, thereby contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation and to combating desertification
11.4.3 Global target 16 – By 2015, the Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization is in force and operational, consistent with national legislation
11.5. Strategic Goal E: Enhance implementation through participatory planning, knowledge management and capacity building
11.5.1. Global target 18 – К By 2020, the traditional knowledge, innovations and practices of indigenous and local communities relevant for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, and their customary use of biological resources, are respected, subject to national legislation and relevant international obligations, and fully integrated and reflected in the implementation of the Convention with the full and effective participation of indigenous and local communities, at all relevant levels
11.5.2. Global target 19 – By 2020, at the latest, the mobilization of financial resources for effectively implementing the Strategic Plan 2011-2020 from all sources and in accordance with the consolidated and agreed process in the Strategy for Resource Mobilization should increase substantially from the current levels. The unified plan for achieving the national development goals of the Russian Federation for the period up to 2024 was approved in order to implement the Decree of the President of the Russian Federation dated May 7, 2018 No. 204 “On national goals and strategic objectives for the development of the Russian Federation for the period until 2024”.

The national development goals of the Russian Federation are of “interprogramme” (“interproject”) nature: the achievement of any of the national goals cannot be ensured within the framework of only one state program and (or) a national project (program). In addition, national development goals are closely interlinked. Achieving some goals is directly dependent on the achievement of others. Thus, halving the poverty level is impossible without sustainable economic growth. Labor productivity growth is not possible without the widespread adoption of digital technology and innovative development.

The unified plan to achieve the national development goals of the Russian Federation for the period up to 2024 represents the trajectory of the indicators characterizing these goals reaching the target levels, as well as a list of tools and mechanisms aimed at their achievement, regardless of belonging to state programs and national projects ( programs).

The government approved the Export Development Strategy for the agricultural engineering industry until 2025 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

The strategy characterizes the state of the industry and determines the basic principles of state policy in the field of supporting the export of agricultural machinery for the medium term.

The draft Strategy was developed in accordance with Federal Law dated June 28, 2014 No. 172-ФЗ “On Strategic Planning in the Russian Federation”, taking into account the Forecast of the Long-Term Socio-Economic Development of the Russian Federation for the Period until 2030, and the Forecast of Scientific and Technological Development of the Russian Federation until 2030 year , government programs "development of industry and increase its competitiveness" , "development of foreign economic activity" , Strategies for development of agricultural engineering of Russia on the item IRS until 2030 (approved by the Decree of the Government on July 7, 2017 No. 1455-p).

The purpose of the Strategy is accelerated export growth in the agricultural engineering industry.

The strategy envisages providing support to Russian manufacturers of agricultural machinery, expanding the range of products, creating conditions for sustainable growth in exports of Russian agricultural machinery products.

Strategy Objectives:

- an increase in the volume of deliveries of products of Russian agricultural engineering in traditional markets;

- expansion of the geography of deliveries of products of Russian agricultural engineering;

- involvement of new domestic manufacturers in export deliveries.

As a result of the implementation of the Strategy, it is planned to increase the volume of export of agricultural machinery - from 10,255 million rubles in 2018 to 30,220 million rubles by 2025. The number of enterprises exporting domestic agricultural machinery products should increase from 48 in 2018 to 70 by 2025 (more than 80% of all domestic enterprises). The number of countries - importers of Russian agricultural engineering products should increase from 35 countries in 2018 to 65 by 2025. It is planned that each of the market segments individually will show a two-fold or more increase in exported products.

The implementation of the Strategy will allow for the formation of a structured approach to solving the key problems facing domestic manufacturers and exporters, and will contribute to an increase in the load of production capacities and production volumes of agricultural machinery, and an increase in demand for raw materials, components and materials of Russian production.

The government approved the Federal Scientific and Technical Program for the Development of Genetic Technologies for 2019–2027 (hereinafter - the Program).

The main goals of the Program are a comprehensive solution to the problems of the accelerated development of genetic technologies, including genetic editing technologies, the creation of scientific and technological reserves for medicine, agriculture and industry, the improvement of the biological emergency prevention and control system in this area.

Directions for the implementation of the Program: biosafety and ensuring technological independence, genetic technologies for the development of agriculture, medicine, industrial microbiology.

The program provides for the creation and development on the basis of scientific and educational organizations of laboratories and centers conducting research in the field of genetic technologies, their technical support, research and development using genetic technologies, including the development of biological drugs, diagnostic systems and immunobiological agents for healthcare, biotechnology for agriculture and industry.

It is expected that as a result of the implementation of the Program, scientific and technological reserves for medicine, agriculture and industry will be created. Using genetic editing technologies, plant and animal lines will be developed, including aquaculture, in demand in the real sector of the economy. It is also planned to develop models of human diseases using genetic technologies in vitro and in vivo, the functioning of bioresource centers that ensure the formation, storage and provision of collection samples in accordance with international standards, the creation of bioinformation and genetic databases, the creation of at least three world-class genomic research centers . The development of biological preparations, diagnostic systems and immunobiological agents for healthcare will be ensured,

The program provides for the formation of a plan for its implementation for each three-year period and a comprehensive research plan. The responsible executor and coordinator of the Program is the Ministry of Education and Science of Russia. Methodological, informational, analytical and organizational support for the implementation of the Program is assigned to the Kurchatov Institute, which is the main scientific organization of the Program.

Implementation of the Program will be financed within the framework of state programs “Scientific and Technological Development of the Russian Federation” (including within the framework of the national project “Science”), “Development of Education”, “Development of Health Care”, “Development of Industry and Increasing Its Competitiveness”, “Development pharmaceutical and medical industry ”for 2013–2020,“ Information Society (2011–2020), ”the State Program for the Development of Agriculture and Regulation of Agricultural Products, Raw Materials and food, as well as due to budgetary appropriations of the budgets of the constituent entities of the Federation and extrabudgetary sources.

The government approved the Strategy for the development of Russian seaports in the Caspian basin, rail and road approaches to them until 2030 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

The Strategy was developed taking into account the Concept of long-term socio-economic development of the Russian Federation for the period until 2020 (approved by the Government Decree of November 17, 2008 No. 1662-r), the Concept for the demographic policy of the Russian Federation for the period until 2025 (approved by Decree of the President of Russia of 9 October 2007 №1351), the national security Strategy of the Russian Federation (approved by the Decree of the President of Russia on December 31, 2015 №683), Program of action for the strategic interests of the Russian F eration in the Caspian region in the 2016-2018 years.

The main goal of the Strategy is to strengthen the economic and geopolitical presence of Russia in the Caspian Sea, expand and deepen economic and cultural ties with the countries of the Caspian basin, create conditions for additional socio-economic development of the Caspian region of Russia by increasing the flow of international trade passing through the ports of the Caspian basin.

Targeted directions for the implementation of the Strategy:

- development of the Russian Caspian transport hub and its inclusion in the international trade system;

- creating a sustainable transport and logistics corridor with Iran, India and the Gulf countries;

- socio-economic development of the Caspian region;

- development of export-oriented business in the Caspian region through the Russian Caspian transport hub;

- reduction of existing logistics costs;

- Strengthening the country's defense and security in the Caspian.

The strategy provides for the solution of regulatory, tariff, investment, operational and institutional tasks.

Regulatory tasks include improving the competitiveness of freight and passenger traffic through Russian Caspian ports by simplifying administrative procedures (including speeding up customs procedures during cargo transportation, prompt coordination of projects to modernize port infrastructure), creating favorable conditions for the development of domestic and international tourism in this region (including simplification of the customs regime).

Tariff tasks - the formation and administration of uniform competitive tariffs for transportation through the Caspian transport hub.

Investment objectives are the modernization of the existing and the creation of a new logistics and transport infrastructure for the development of freight and passenger transportation, including port infrastructure, as well as long and near road and rail approaches to seaports.

Operational objectives - the introduction of a planning and project management system that reveals the export potential of the Caspian region, in particular production and logistics clusters, by creating the necessary legislative and administrative conditions and institutions.

Institutional tasks are the creation of incentives for the development of agriculture and industrial production, which, together with the development of transport infrastructure, can provide a synergistic effect for the development of the region, including the formation of development institutions and support for such projects.

The strategy is planned to be implemented in three stages: the first stage (until 2020) - preparatory, the second stage (2020–2025) - the main, the third stage (2026–2030) - promising.

Target directions, tasks, mechanisms for implementing the Strategy are aimed at creating a sustainable transport and logistics corridor, developing trade and tourism, primarily with Iran, India and the Persian Gulf countries. As part of the promising stage of the Strategy implementation, it is planned to study the issue of developing trade relations with all the Caspian countries, taking into account the expansion of the capacities of the new deep-sea port (terminal).

The implementation of the Strategy and the fulfillment of its indicators will allow to ensure grain export volumes through the ports of the Caspian basin up to 7 million tons by 2030, and the volume of freight traffic on other dry cargoes up to 7 million tons; to attract the Russian tourist flow to the Caspian region - up to 30 thousand people a year; create more than 2 thousand new jobs.

The government approved the Strategy for the Development of the Forestry Complex of the Russian Federation until 2030 (hereinafter - the Strategy). This is an industry strategic planning document that defines goals and objectives, ways to achieve them, priorities, stages of implementation of state policy in the field of forestry development in Russia.

The strategy is aimed at increasing the long-term competitiveness of the forest industry, increasing the contribution of the forest sector to the country's socio-economic development, the efficient use, protection, reproduction of forests by achieving sustainable forest management.

The main directions of the Strategy are the development of export-oriented production of pulp, the growth of the production of container board and sanitary products for the domestic market, the development of the production of lumber, plywood-plate production, furniture, and wooden housing construction, oriented equally to the domestic market.

By 2030, it is planned to significantly increase the contribution of the forest sector to the country's economy. An increase in the added value created by industry enterprises is expected in the amount of up to 676 billion rubles; increase in the contribution of the forest complex to gross domestic product from 0.5% to 1%; an increase in tax revenues to budgets of all levels from 91 to 189 billion rubles.

The implementation of the Strategy will allow the formation of an economically sustainable, globally competitive group of industries that provides domestic demand for forest products that is built into the world market and the international division of labor and operates on the basis of sustainable forest management and the preservation of the biosphere role of forests.

The government approved the Engineering Development Strategy for the food and processing industry until 2030 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

Providing food and processing industries with modern and high-tech domestic equipment is a necessary condition for increasing the competitiveness of products, maintaining the country's food security and developing export potential.

The goal of the Strategy is to triple the volume of sales of domestic products by 2030.

The strategy provides for an increase in the share of domestic machinery and equipment for the food and processing industry in the domestic market to 62%, an increase in export deliveries by at least 10% annually, an increase in the share of costs for research and development in the total revenue of enterprises of at least than up to 2%. The strategy is planned to be implemented in three stages.

The strategy is planned to be implemented within the framework of the state program “Development of industry and increasing its competitiveness” and the national project “International Cooperation and Export”.

The implementation of the Strategy will contribute to the opening of new production capacities, the creation of high-performance jobs, the technological independence of the food industry from imported engineering products, and the growth of export deliveries of Russian machines.

The main objective of the Programme, which updates and replaces measures of the previous State Policy on Energy Efficiency Increase through the Use of Renewables for the Period up to 2020 (2009), is to “ensure reliable supply of the country’s fuel and energy resources, increase the efficiency of their use, and reduce of anthropogenic impacts of the energy sector on the environment”.

This new version keeps the target of a 40% decrease of energy intensity of the economy between 2007 and 2020, but alters the 4.5% share of electricity generation from renewable energy sources target to 2.5% by 2020 (excluding large hydro over 25 MW). The Programme calls for diverse measures to attain those targets, including:
– evaluating the technological and economic potential of efficient renewables use
– providing subsidies from the state budget in order to compensate for the costs of grid connection for renewables
– installation of smart meters (18.9% of metering devices by 2020)
– increasing the availability of energy infrastructure – reducing the number of steps required to gain access to the grid (from 8 to 5) and reducing the delay of connection to the grid (from 276 to 40 days)
– raising public awareness on energy conservation and energy efficiency.

The State Programme is composed of seven sub-programmes:
– SP1: Energy conservation and energy efficiency improvement
– SP2: Development and modernisation of the power industry
– SP3: Development of the oil industry
– SP4: Development of the gas industry
– SP5: Restructuring and development of the coal industry
– SP6: Development of renewable energy
– SP7: Ensuring the implementation of the state programme.

The objectives of the Strategy are to ensure sustainable and balanced spatial development of Russia, reduce inter-regional differences in the level and quality of life of people, accelerate the pace of economic growth and technological development, ensure national security.

The strategy defines the tasks, principles, priorities and main directions of the spatial development of Russia, the scenarios of spatial development, including the priority (target) scenario, promising centers of economic growth, macro-regions, promising economic specializations of the constituent entities of the Federation, target indicators of spatial development of Russia.

As part of the implementation of the Strategy, it is planned to increase the availability and quality of the main transport, energy, information and telecommunication infrastructure, reduce the level of inter-regional differentiation in the socio-economic development of the constituent entities of the Federation, reduce intra-regional socio-economic differences, expand geography and accelerate economic growth, scientific, technological and innovative development of Russia due to the socio-economic development of promising centers of economic Skogen growth, outstripping the average Russian rates of socio-economic development of the Far East, to ensure sustainable growth of the resident population in this macro-region.

The list of promising centers of economic growth includes promising cities that form large urban agglomerations and the largest urban agglomerations, which will provide a contribution to economic growth of more than 1% annually (20 centers); promising centers for economic growth of the constituent entities of the Federation, which will provide a contribution to economic growth from 0.2% to 1% annually (44 centers); promising centers for economic growth of the constituent entities of the Federation, which will provide a contribution to economic growth of up to 0.2% annually (31 centers); promising mineral resources and agro-industrial centers (27 centers); promising centers of economic growth, in which conditions have arisen for the formation of world-class scientific and educational centers (20 centers).

The strategy provides for the creation of a new mechanism for the development of territories (investment sites) with a special regime for doing business, taking into account the promising specializations of the subjects of the Federation and other features of the territories. In order to avoid duplication of state support measures, federal authorities with state support for the sectors of the economy of each specific subject of the Federation will take into account promising economic specializations of the subjects of the Federation bordering on it and which are part of one macroregion.

Infrastructural support for the socio-economic development of territories will be carried out as part of the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan for the Modernization and Expansion of the Main Infrastructure until 2024 (approved by Government Decree No. 2101-r of September 30, 2018, hereinafter referred to as the Comprehensive Plan) and national projects.

In order to mandatory include measures of the comprehensive plan and comprehensive plans for the development of infrastructure of the constituent entities of the Federation in the investment programs of natural monopoly entities, the Government of Russia will develop a procedure for the approval and approval of investment programs (plans) of natural monopoly entities, including, among other things, participation in such coordination of executive bodies of the constituent entities of the Federation.

As part of the implementation of the Strategy, it is also planned to develop and approve a set of measures to attract people in areas with significant economic potential, characterized by an unfavorable demographic situation, by stimulating internal and external migration.

COVID-19: The government adopted "Methodical Recommendations No. МР 2.3.0171-20 Food Hygiene. Specialized diet for children and adults in self-isolation or quarantine at home in connection with COVID-19." 

These guidelines are directed on the possibility of elimination or considerable decrease in negative influence of the specified factors on the health of the population by optimization of nutrition and food consumption in connection with COVID-19 and can be used by citizens, doctors-dieticians, experts of bodies and organizations of Federal Service for Supervision of Consumer Rights Protection and Human Welfare and other persons and organizations concerned. In order to maintain normal body weight and maintain balanced body composition, it is necessary to maintain a full, adequate diet with a caloric value reduction of 200-400 kcal compared to the usual diet. At the same time, it is important to preserve the maximum variety of foodstuffs - sources of protein, fats, carbohydrates, and micronutrients, to ensure the consumption of water at least 2 liters per day. Indicatively, a child of preschool age needs at least 1 liter of free liquid per day, and children from 12 to 18 years old need 1.5 liters. All drinking water and all beverages in the diet should be considered. It is recommended to include all major traditional products in the diet: (a) bread, flour, cereals; (b) milk and dairy products; (c) meat, poultry products and fish products (fish products must be included in the diet at least twice a week); (d) oils; (e) eggs; and (f) sufficient fresh fruits and vegetables.

By this time, domestic consumption should reach around 86.2 million tons per year, while exports of grains, legumes and products of their processing should reach 55.9 million tons versus 54.9 million tons of similar exports in 2018.

The strategy envisages around 281 billion rubles (or around $4.3 billion) of investment into various infrastructure projects, including the building of grain terminals in Russian seaports, and some storage facilities for grain and feed. These investments should improve logistics in the Russian grain and feed industries, according to the document. An additional 3.3 trillion rubles (over $50 billion) are to be invested in the purchasing of new agricultural equipment, including harvesters and tractors. These are private investments, as the strategy provides no details regarding the planned state aid to Russian grain producers during the coming years. The Strategy was developed in accordance with the Federal Law of June 28, 2014 No. 172-ФЗ “On Strategic Planning in the Russian Federation” taking into account the Economic Security Strategy of the Russian Federation for the period until 2030 (approved by Decree of the President of Russia dated May 13, 2017 No. 208) , Strategies for the development of the information society in the Russian Federation for 2017–2030 (approved by Decree of the President of Russia dated May 9, 2017 No. 203), Strategies for the environmental safety of the Russian Federation for the period until 2025 (approved by Decree of the President and Russia dated April 19, 2017 No. 176) and other strategic planning documents.

The strategy determines the priorities, goals and objectives of the geological industry, aimed at sustainable supply of minerals to the needs of the Russian economy, including export obligations. The strategy is the basis for the formation and implementation of state policy in the field of geological exploration of the subsoil, reproduction and use of the mineral resource base at the federal and regional levels.

For the purposes of the Strategy, a mineral resource base is a combination of explored and estimated mineral reserves, as well as localized and predicted resources.

The strategy provides for increasing the mineral resource base by increasing the investment attractiveness of geological exploration at all stages, increasing the quality of forecasting and searching for new deposits, increasing the efficiency of developing known, including undeveloped, deposits by introducing modern technologies for processing, integrated mineral extraction , increasing the level of geological exploration of the country.

In accordance with the needs of the economy, the economic conditions of development and the geological prospects of building up, all strategic and most significant types of minerals are divided into three groups: minerals, the provision of reserves of which under any scenario of economic development will satisfy the necessary needs until 2035 and beyond; minerals, the achieved production levels of which are not adequately provided with reserves of developed deposits for the period until 2035; scarce minerals, the domestic consumption of which is largely provided by forced imports and / or stockpiles.

For each of these groups of minerals, the indicators of reproduction of their reserves are determined, taking into account the state of the resource base and the rate of repayment in the bowels. The reproduction of mineral reserves is envisaged on the basis of intensification of regional geological study of the subsoil, intensification of exploration and subsequent stages, taking into account the geological prospects and territorial features of the country's development.

The strategy also provides for economic incentives for geological exploration of the subsoil, reproduction and development of the mineral resource base, the formation of a system of information, scientific, technological and personnel support for the development of the mineral resource base.

For the development of new industrial territories, support is provided for geological exploration of the early stages at the expense of the federal budget and the creation of a special tax regime to attract private investment.

Within the framework of the Strategy, it is planned to develop planning for geological exploration within the natural boundaries of the mineralogical provinces and mineral resource centers, distinguished taking into account the possibilities of transport and energy infrastructure of the territories.

The implementation of the Strategy is foreseen in two stages.

At the first stage (until 2024), in particular, it is planned to increase state funding for large-scale regional geological explorations, create a unified fund of geological information on the subsoil, develop the necessary program and design documents to ensure the concentration of financial resources, technological and human potential to achieve indicators of the development of mineral raw materials base. At the end of the first stage, the Strategy will be updated based on the results achieved and the forecast of mining for the period after 2024.

At the second stage (2025–2035), it is planned to continue the work necessary to increase the investment attractiveness of Russian subsoil. Based on this, a model of a self-regulatory system to achieve the optimal balance of growth and repayment of mineral reserves will be created. It is also planned to complete the transformations associated with improving the system for collecting, processing, analyzing, storing and providing geological information for use, and strengthening scientific, technical and personnel support for geological exploration.

The strategy is aimed, inter alia, at improving the scientific and technical support for geological exploration, increasing the availability of geological organizations with geological specialists on the basis of the development and implementation of a training and retraining program.
policy_description: Strategy for the development of the mineral resource base of Russia until 2035

policydecision_details: The President signed Russia’s Food Security Doctrine. The Doctrine is a framework document that outlines Russia’s agricultural production and policy goals. In accordance with the Doctrine, Russia established the following minimum self-sufficiency targets: 95 percent in grain and potatoes, 90 percent in milk and dairy products, 85 percent in meat and meat products and 80 percent in sugar, vegetable oil, and fish products. The Doctrine also underlines the necessity to guarantee food safety. It does not address funding or provide any concrete government measures for reaching its targets. However, it will be a vehicle which could lead to both opportunities and obstacles for U.S. agricultural exports.
contextoradditionalinfo: The Doctrine lists measures aimed at poverty alleviation, improvement of domestic market infrastructure, building of the national material reserves, and enforcing Russian food safety laws. Concerning food safety issues, the Doctrine specifically highlights products derived from genetically modified sources and the need to control these products (Articles 12, 18). In the reference to foreign trade (Articles 15 and 16) it notes that policy should be developed which is consistent with food security criteria. Specifically it states that it may be necessary to revise tariff measures to “rationalize the ratio” of imports and exports. It also justifies corrective action to when foreign governments dump or use export subsidies to access the Russian market. However it also cautions that when implementing sanitary, veterinary and phytosanitary controls, international standards need to be taken into consideration.

COVID-19: On 26 March 2020, a Federal Law came into force allowing the Russian government to set maximum prices for any medicines and medical devices for up to 90 days in case of an emergency or the threat of the spread of dangerous diseases (including COVID-19).

According to the new Law, if after 30 days of monitoring retail prices for pharmaceuticals and medical devices the government detects price increases of 30% or more, it can then introduce restrictions on the prices of these products.

In particular, the government will have the right to determine, for a period of up to 90 days, a list of medicines and medical devices for which it can set manufacturers’ maximum selling prices and maximum wholesale and retail mark-ups.

Maximum prices set by the government will apply to manufacturers, distributors and pharmacies.

It is important to note that this right is granted to the government for any medicine and medical device without exception.

In addition, the Russian State Duma is considering a bill to increase penalties and sanctions for any company violating these rules.

The government approved the Export Development Strategy for the agricultural engineering industry until 2025 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

The strategy characterizes the state of the industry and determines the basic principles of state policy in the field of supporting the export of agricultural machinery for the medium term.

The draft Strategy was developed in accordance with Federal Law dated June 28, 2014 No. 172-ФЗ “On Strategic Planning in the Russian Federation”, taking into account the Forecast of the Long-Term Socio-Economic Development of the Russian Federation for the Period until 2030, and the Forecast of Scientific and Technological Development of the Russian Federation until 2030 year , government programs "development of industry and increase its competitiveness" , "development of foreign economic activity" , Strategies for development of agricultural engineering of Russia on the item IRS until 2030 (approved by the Decree of the Government on July 7, 2017 No. 1455-p).

The purpose of the Strategy is accelerated export growth in the agricultural engineering industry.

The strategy envisages providing support to Russian manufacturers of agricultural machinery, expanding the range of products, creating conditions for sustainable growth in exports of Russian agricultural machinery products.

Strategy Objectives:

- an increase in the volume of deliveries of products of Russian agricultural engineering in traditional markets;

- expansion of the geography of deliveries of products of Russian agricultural engineering;

- involvement of new domestic manufacturers in export deliveries.

As a result of the implementation of the Strategy, it is planned to increase the volume of export of agricultural machinery - from 10,255 million rubles in 2018 to 30,220 million rubles by 2025. The number of enterprises exporting domestic agricultural machinery products should increase from 48 in 2018 to 70 by 2025 (more than 80% of all domestic enterprises). The number of countries - importers of Russian agricultural engineering products should increase from 35 countries in 2018 to 65 by 2025. It is planned that each of the market segments individually will show a two-fold or more increase in exported products.

The implementation of the Strategy will allow for the formation of a structured approach to solving the key problems facing domestic manufacturers and exporters, and will contribute to an increase in the load of production capacities and production volumes of agricultural machinery, and an increase in demand for raw materials, components and materials of Russian production.

The main objective of the Programme, which updates and replaces measures of the previous State Policy on Energy Efficiency Increase through the Use of Renewables for the Period up to 2020 (2009), is to “ensure reliable supply of the country’s fuel and energy resources, increase the efficiency of their use, and reduce of anthropogenic impacts of the energy sector on the environment”.

This new version keeps the target of a 40% decrease of energy intensity of the economy between 2007 and 2020, but alters the 4.5% share of electricity generation from renewable energy sources target to 2.5% by 2020 (excluding large hydro over 25 MW). The Programme calls for diverse measures to attain those targets, including:
– evaluating the technological and economic potential of efficient renewables use
– providing subsidies from the state budget in order to compensate for the costs of grid connection for renewables
– installation of smart meters (18.9% of metering devices by 2020)
– increasing the availability of energy infrastructure – reducing the number of steps required to gain access to the grid (from 8 to 5) and reducing the delay of connection to the grid (from 276 to 40 days)
– raising public awareness on energy conservation and energy efficiency.

The State Programme is composed of seven sub-programmes:
– SP1: Energy conservation and energy efficiency improvement
– SP2: Development and modernisation of the power industry
– SP3: Development of the oil industry
– SP4: Development of the gas industry
– SP5: Restructuring and development of the coal industry
– SP6: Development of renewable energy
– SP7: Ensuring the implementation of the state programme.

Strategic Goals:

11.1. Strategic Goal A: Address the underlying causes of biodiversity loss by mainstreaming biodiversity across government and society
11.1.1 Global target 1 – By 2020, at the latest, people are aware of the values of biodiversity and the steps they can take to conserve and use it sustainably
11.1.2 Global target 2 – By 2020, at the latest, biodiversity values have been integrated into national and local development and poverty reduction strategies and planning processes and are being incorporated into national accounting, as appropriate, and reporting systems
11.1.3 Global target 3 – By 2020, at the latest, incentives, including subsidies, harmful to biodiversity are eliminated, phased out or reformed in order to minimize or avoid negative impacts, and positive incentives for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity are developed and applied, consistent and in harmony with the Convention and other relevant international obligations, taking into account national socio-economic conditions
11.1.4 Global target 4 – By 2020, at the latest, Governments, business and stakeholders at all levels have taken steps to achieve or have implemented plans for sustainable production and consumption and have kept the impacts of use of natural resources well within safe ecological limits
11.2. Strategic Goal B: Reduce the direct pressures on biodiversity and promote sustainable use
11.2.1 Global target 5 – By 2020, the rate of loss of all natural habitats, including forests, is at least halved and where feasible brought close to zero, and degradation and fragmentation is significantly reduced
11.2.2 Global Target 6 – By 2020 all fish and invertebrate stocks and aquatic plants are managed and harvested sustainably, legally and applying ecosystem based approaches, so that overfishing is avoided, recovery plans and measures are in place for all depleted species, fisheries have no significant adverse impacts on threatened species and vulnerable ecosystems and the impacts of fisheries on stocks, species and ecosystems are within safe ecological limits 
11.2.3 Global target 7 – By 2020 areas under agriculture, aquaculture and forestry are managed sustainably, ensuring conservation of biodiversity 
11.2.4 Global target 8 – By 2020, pollution, including from excess nutrients, has been brought to levels that are not detrimental to ecosystem function and biodiversity 
11.2.5 Global target 9 – By 2020, invasive alien species and pathways are identified and prioritized, priority species are controlled or eradicated, and measures are in place to manage pathways to prevent their introduction and establishment 
11.2.6 Global target 10 – By 2015, the multiple anthropogenic pressures on coral reefs, and other vulnerable ecosystems impacted by climate change or ocean acidification are minimized, so as to maintain their integrity and functioning 
11.3. Strategic Goal C: Improve the status of biodiversity by safeguarding ecosystems, species and genetic diversity 
11.3.1 Global target 11 – By 2020, at least 17 per cent of terrestrial and inland water, and 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas, especially areas of particular importance for biodiversity and ecosystem services, are conserved through effectively and equitably managed, ecologically representative and well connected systems of protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures, and integrated into the wider landscape and seascapes 
11.3.2 Global target 12 – By 2020, the genetic diversity of cultivated plants and farmed and domesticated animals and of wild relatives, including other socio-economically as well as culturally valuable species, is maintained, and strategies have been developed and implemented for minimizing genetic erosion and safeguarding their genetic diversity
11.2.2 11.3.2 Global target 13: By 2020, the genetic diversity of cultivated plants and farmed and domesticated animals and of wild relatives, including other socio-economically as well as culturally valuable species, is maintained, and strategies have been developed and implemented for minimizing genetic erosion and safeguarding their genetic diversity
11.4. Strategic Goal D: Enhance the benefits to all from biodiversity and ecosystem services
11.4.1 Global target 14 – By 2020, ecosystems that provide essential services, including services related to water, and contribute to health, livelihoods and wellbeing, are restored and safeguarded, taking into account the needs of women, indigenous and local communities, and the poor and vulnerable
11.4.2. Global target 15 – By 2020, ecosystem resilience and the contribution of biodiversity to carbon stocks has been enhanced, through conservation and restoration, including restoration of at least 15 per cent of degraded ecosystems, thereby contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation and to combating desertification
11.4.3 Global target 16 – By 2015, the Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from their Utilization is in force and operational, consistent with national legislation
11.5. Strategic Goal E: Enhance implementation through participatory planning, knowledge management and capacity building
11.5.1. Global target 18 – К By 2020, the traditional knowledge, innovations and practices of indigenous and local communities relevant for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, and their customary use of biological resources, are respected, subject to national legislation and relevant international obligations, and fully integrated and reflected in the implementation of the Convention with the full and effective participation of indigenous and local communities, at all relevant levels

Global target 19 – By 2020, at the latest, the mobilization of financial resources for effectively implementing the Strategic Plan 2011-2020 from all sources and in accordance with the consolidated and agreed process in the Strategy for Resource Mobilization should increase substantially from the current levels. Development programs were adopted for 15 leading universities in the framework of the 5–100 project, the Presidential Program for Advanced Training of Engineering Personnel, the Program for Supporting Citizens Admitted to Leading Foreign Educational Organizations, and Global Education.

The innovative development programs of 60 largest companies with state participation were approved, 35 technological platforms were created, a system of grants and support for borrowed financing of innovative business projects was formed as part of the state program "Industrial Development and Increasing Its Competitiveness" and the activities of development institutions.

Development institutions have created an integrated system for supporting promising projects at key stages of development.

The state academies of sciences were reorganized, the Russian Science Foundation, the Foundation for Advanced Research were created, and the national research center "N.E. Zhukovsky Institute" was formed. The program of fundamental scientific research of state academies of sciences for 2013–2020 was approved ( Government Decree of December 3, 2012 No. 2237-r ).

Implementation of action plans (roadmaps) for the development of new industries has begun.

In the direction of supporting the territories of innovative development, 25 pilot innovative territorial clusters located in 20 regions of the Federation have been formed.

To solve the problems of the second stage of the Strategy, a signed decree approved a plan for its implementation in 2015–2016 (hereinafter referred to as the Plan). It provides for measures to improve the education system, popularize scientific, scientific, technical and innovative activities, form a state support system for the scientific and technical creativity of children and youth, ensure effective implementation of innovative development programs of companies with state participation, create mechanisms to stimulate demand for innovations, and modernize the structure research and development sector, development of financial infrastructure for innovation, create mechanisms for supporting legal protection of the results of promising commercial developments of Russian innovative companies.

In 2013, the government adopted the Methodological Recommendation for Emergency Situations (Plan), whose components related to nutrition are the following:

The type of life support of the population in the emergency zone; the type of ZhON in the emergency zone (activities to satisfy any primary need of the population in the emergency zone). Note- The types of life support of the population include medical support, water, food, housing, utilities, basic necessities, transport and information support

Supply of food and water to the affected population in disaster areas, evacuation areas and forces involved in emergency response is based on the physiological principle for the unemployed (and energy sufficiency)

The daily needs of the affected population for food, water, utilities, household fuel are calculated according to its predicted number and standards of emergency support. The total need for these types of livelihoods by multiplying daily requirements by the length of the primary life support period

When assessing the needs of the affected population for food, it should be considered that in the first 1.2 days after the disaster, before organizing the preparation of hot food in the emergency zone, it will be possible to use only dry rations, canned and other products that do not require heat treatment. Bread will need to be delivered from neighboring settlements by any means of transport. It is necessary to take into account the need to deliver ready-made baby food to infants and children up to 2 years of age, and for some categories of patients, special nutrition before their urgent evacuation from the emergency zone. In determining the volumes necessary for the affected population of bread, meat and fish products, potatoes, vegetables, pasta and cereals, fats, sugar, salt should be based on the need to organize two hot meals a day and once a day, canned foods or prefabricated rations. The food supply standards are given in tables P 1.1, P 1.2, P 1.5 of appendix1.

Upon receipt of information on the possible evacuation of the population in the evacuation areas, the condition of the housing stock of settlements and the degree of their readiness to receive the evacuated population shall be clarified: condition of water sources and water supply systems and their capabilities: condition of public catering and trade points, their production capacities.

The population who received severe and moderate lesions as a result of the accident after providing emergency medical care at specially developed medical centers is sent to medical institutions where they are provided with treatment and nutrition according to special diets of medical nutrition.

policydecision_details:
The government approved the Amber Industry Development Strategy for the period up to 2025 (hereinafter - the Strategy).

The strategy contains an analysis of the Russian amber industry, the goals and main principles of state policy in the amber industry, a forecast of domestic demand for amber products, and economic indicators of the industry's development.

The strategy is planned to be implemented in two stages.

At the first stage (2017–2018), it is planned to solve the problems of preserving the potential of the industry and reducing the negative impact of adverse external economic conditions. It is planned to launch tools and measures of state support. This will save industrial assets, qualified personnel of the industry. It is planned to increase the processing of amber raw materials in Russia.

At the second stage (2019–2025), it is expected to achieve the level of leading countries in terms of finished product output and added value when processing amber raw materials. Amber enterprises will use the best available technology.

The strategy provides for a phased increase in such target indicators as the extraction of amber raw materials, the production of amber processed products, employment in the field of amber processing, the number of functioning tourist and cultural sites associated with amber.

As a result of the implementation of the Strategy, the processing of amber raw materials in Russia will increase, export opportunities of the industry enterprises will increase, and conditions will be created for technological modernization of enterprises.
policy_description: Amber Industry Development Strategy for the period until 2025

policydecision_details: The Ministry of Agriculture of the Russian Federation has revised upwards the minimum prices for 2015 wheat crop purchases by the State Intervention Fund. contextoradditionalinfo: The new prices of milling wheat classes 3 and 4 were increased by some 14 percent and 18 percent from their previous levels set in March, respectively, and are the highest in the past ten years. policydecision_details: This doctrine is a system of views on the purpose, principles, content and ways of implementing a unified state policy of the Russian Federation within the country and in the international arena on issues related to climate change and its consequences. The strategic objective of climate policy is to ensure the safe and sustainable development of the Russian Federation, including the institutional, economic, environmental and social, including demographic aspects of development in a changing climate and the occurrence of relevant threats. The basic principles of climate policy are: the global nature of the Russian Federation's interests in relation to climate change and its effects; priority of national interests in the development and implementation of climate policy; clarity and disclosure policies; recognition of the need for action both within the country and within the framework of a full-fledged international partnership; comprehensiveness of accounting and possible loss of benefits associated with climate change; precaution in planning and implementing measures to ensure the security of the person, and the state of the economy from the adverse effects of climate change.
policy_description: Climate doctrine of the Russian Federation
contextoradditionalinfo: The main areas of climate policy are: 1) the development of the legal framework and organization of state regulation in the field of climate change; 2) development of economic mechanisms related to the implementation of adaptation measures and mitigation of human impact on the climate; 3) scientific, informational and staffing for the development and implementation of adaptation measures and mitigation of human impact on the climate; 4) international cooperation in the development and implementation of adaptation measures and mitigation of human impact on the climate.

policydecision_details: The Government is restricting the import of poultry from Ukraine to Crimea, allegedly over concerns regarding avian influenza (AI). Only a limited number of certified companies are allowed to export their poultry to Crimea.
